items.stem: A student claims: "The energy released in fission comes from the neutrons’ kinetic energy." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It comes from the increase in binding energy (decrease in mass) as the heavy nucleus splits into more tightly bound fragments.
items.markingKey: It comes from the increase in binding energy (decrease in mass) as the heavy nucleus splits into more tightly bound fragments. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why a mass of uranium below the critical mass cannot sustain a chain reaction.
items.answer: In a small mass the surface area is large compared with the volume, so many neutrons escape before causing fission; fewer than one neutron per fission goes on to cause another fission (k < 1) and the reaction dies out. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In a small mass the surface area is large compared with the volume, so many neutrons escape before causing fission; fewer than one neutron per fission goes on to cause another fission (k < 1) and the reaction dies out. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A reactor has an effective neutron multiplication factor k = 0.98 and an effective generation time of 0.00100 s. (a) State whether the reactor is subcritical, critical or supercritical. (b) Determine the factor by which the fission rate changes in 5.0 s. (c) Explain the role of delayed neutrons in making the reactor controllable, and how operators would respond.
items.answer: (a) subcritical; (b) ×1.35 × 10⁻⁴⁴; (c) delayed neutrons from fission-product decay lengthen the effective generation time to ~0.1 s, giving time for control-rod adjustment
items.markingKey: (a) k < 1 → subcritical (A1). (b) number of generations = 5000 (M1); factor = k^n = 1.35 × 10⁻⁴⁴ (A1). (c) delayed neutrons (R1); operators insert/withdraw rods to restore k = 1 (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Fission triggered when a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 absorbs a (usually slow) neutron"?
items.answer: neutron-induced fission
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of neutron-induced fission.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "nuclear fission"?
options: An engineered facility hundreds of metres underground in stable rock for long-term isolation of high-level waste
The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller nuclei of comparable mass, with the release of neutrons and energy
Rods of a strong neutron absorber (boron or cadmium) moved into or out of the core to control the rate of fission
Severe overheating of a reactor core so that the fuel melts, usually after failure of cooling
items.answer: The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller nuclei of comparable mass, with the release of neutrons and energy
items.markingKey: B. "nuclear fission" is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller nuclei of comparable mass, with the release of neutrons and energy.

items.stem: Explain the difference between spontaneous fission and neutron-induced fission.
items.answer: Spontaneous fission happens randomly without an external trigger (rare except in very heavy nuclides); induced fission follows absorption of a neutron, forming an excited compound nucleus (e.g. U-236) that splits.
items.markingKey: Spontaneous fission happens randomly without an external trigger (rare except in very heavy nuclides); induced fission follows absorption of a neutron, forming an excited compound nucleus (e.g. U-236) that splits. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is the critical mass smaller for a sphere than for a flat sheet of the same material?

items.answer: a sphere has the smallest surface area for its volume, so fewer neutrons escape

items.stem: A teacher in Melbourne asks a class to choose the one correct statement about spontaneous and neutron-induced fission; chain reactions. Which statement should be chosen?

It splits mainly into two medium-mass fragments plus 2–3 neutrons.
In a nuclear power station, the reactor produces electricity directly.
In fission the uranium nucleus breaks into many small pieces like an explosion of protons and neutrons.
items.answer: It splits mainly into two medium-mass fragments plus 2–3 neutrons.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. It splits mainly into two medium-mass fragments plus 2–3 neutrons.

items.stem: Explain why slow (thermal) neutrons are more effective than fast neutrons at causing fission of uranium-235.
items.answer: The probability (cross-section) of absorption by U-235 is far greater for slow neutrons, which spend longer near the nucleus; fast neutrons tend to scatter or pass through.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The probability (cross-section) of absorption by U-235 is far greater for slow neutrons, which spend longer near the nucleus; fast neutrons tend to scatter or pass through. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

If 5.00 × 10²⁰ uranium-235 nuclei undergo fission, each releasing 180 MeV, how much energy is released?

Fission of U-235 typically releases about 200 MeV per event. (a) Explain the origin of this energy using the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve (U-235 ≈ 7.6 MeV, fragments ≈ 8.5 MeV). (b) Use these values to estimate the energy released. (c) Account for the forms in which the energy appears and explain why not all of it can be used in a power station.
items.answer: (a) Fragments are more tightly bound than uranium, so total binding energy increases; the increase equals the energy released. (b) ≈ 235 × (8.5 − 7.6) ≈ 210 MeV. (c) ~165 MeV kinetic energy of fragments, ~5 MeV neutrons, ~7 MeV prompt γ, plus delayed β and γ from fragment decay and ~10 MeV carried by antineutrinos that escape; the thermal energy is converted to electricity with ~33 % efficiency (second law of thermodynamics).
items.markingKey: Binding-energy argument (R1); estimate ≈ 200 MeV (M1 A1); forms of energy including neutrinos (R1); efficiency limitation (R1).

items.stem: Uranium-235 undergoes the fission ¹₀n + ²³⁵U → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3 ¹₀n. Binding energies per nucleon: U-235 7.591 MeV, Ba-141 8.326 MeV, Kr-92 8.513 MeV. (a) Calculate the energy released per fission. (b) Determine the energy released if 2.0 kg of U-235 undergoes this fission. (c) Calculate the mass converted to energy and express it as a percentage of the fuel mass. (d) Explain why the released energy is mostly kinetic energy of the fragments.
items.answer: (a) 173 MeV; (b) 1.42 × 10¹⁴ J; (c) 0.00158 kg (0.079 %); (d) Coulomb repulsion between the two positively charged fragments

items.stem: "Meitner and Frisch’s interpretation of Hahn and Strassmann’s results is a model case of collaboration in science." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It illustrates productive interdisciplinary collaboration and also how social factors affect credit in science (NOS).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: chemists detected barium; physicists explained it using the liquid-drop model and E = mc²; shows the value of international communication. Arguments against: Meitner was excluded from the Nobel Prize, raising issues of recognition and gender bias; political circumstances (exile) shaped the collaboration. Supported judgement: It illustrates productive interdisciplinary collaboration and also how social factors affect credit in science (NOS). items.stem: Explain the role of the thick concrete and steel shielding around a reactor.
items.answer: The core emits intense neutron and gamma radiation; dense concrete and steel absorb these, protecting workers and the environment.

items.stem: "The moderator absorbs neutrons to control the reaction rate." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The moderator slows neutrons; absorption is the job of the control rods. A good moderator absorbs as few neutrons as possible.

items.stem: Describe the energy transfers in a pressurised-water nuclear power station, from fission in the core to electrical energy, and explain the role of the moderator, control rods, coolant, heat exchanger and shielding.
items.answer: Fission converts nuclear (binding) energy into kinetic energy of fragments, which becomes internal energy of the fuel; the coolant (pressurised water) carries it to the heat exchanger, where water in the secondary circuit boils; steam drives turbines (kinetic) and generators (electrical); waste heat is rejected in cooling towers. Moderator slows neutrons for efficient fission; control rods absorb neutrons to keep k = 1; coolant removes heat and keeps fuel safe; heat exchanger isolates radioactive primary water; shielding absorbs neutrons and gamma rays.
items.markingKey: Correct chain of energy transfers (A1 A1); moderator (R1); control rods (R1); coolant and heat exchanger (R1); shielding (R1).

items.stem: Define the term "moderator".
items.answer: A material (such as water or graphite) that slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds by elastic collisions so that they are more likely to cause fission

items.stem: Explain the difference between the control rods and the moderator.
items.answer: The moderator slows neutrons (without absorbing them) to make fission more likely; control rods absorb neutrons to reduce the number available for fission.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a reactor is designed to operate with a multiplication factor of exactly 1.
items.answer: With k = 1 each fission causes one further fission on average, so the power output is steady; k > 1 would make the power grow, k < 1 would shut down the reaction.

items.stem: Explain why the moderator slows neutrons by elastic collisions and why light nuclei are best.
items.answer: In an elastic collision kinetic energy and momentum are conserved; a neutron colliding with a nucleus of similar mass (e.g. hydrogen) can transfer most of its kinetic energy, whereas with a heavy nucleus it bounces off with nearly the same speed.

items.stem: Compare the Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011) accidents in terms of their physical causes, the role of decay heat and reactor design, and the lessons learned for reactor safety.
items.answer: Chernobyl: an RBMK graphite-moderated reactor with a positive void coefficient; during a low-power test with safety systems disabled and most control rods withdrawn, steam voids raised reactivity, causing a power surge, steam explosion and graphite fire with large releases. Fukushima: boiling-water reactors shut down correctly when the earthquake struck, but the tsunami destroyed backup power, so decay heat (several % of full power) could not be removed; cores melted and hydrogen explosions released radioactivity. Lessons: inherent negative feedback (negative void coefficient), robust passive cooling and multiple independent power supplies, siting against natural hazards, independent regulation and safety culture.
items.markingKey: Chernobyl cause including void coefficient (R1 R1); Fukushima cause including decay heat (R1 R1); comparison of design factors (R1); lessons (A1).

(b) Determine the number of Cs-137 nuclei present. (c) Calculate the time for its activity to fall to 4.0 × 10¹² Bq. (d) Explain why cooling ponds are used for the first few years.

items.stem: Evaluate deep geological disposal as a solution for high-level nuclear waste, referring to the half-lives involved, the engineered and natural barriers, and the ethical issue of responsibility to future generations.
items.answer: Waste contains fission products (Cs-137, Sr-90, ~30 y) and actinides (Pu-239, 24 100 y), so isolation for ~10⁵ years is needed. Multiple barriers: vitrified waste or ceramic fuel, corrosion-resistant canisters (copper/steel), bentonite clay buffer, and stable rock with slow groundwater flow. Strengths: passive safety, no need for active management; Finland’s Onkalo is operating. Limitations: uncertainty in predicting geology and climate over 100 000 years, communicating danger to future people, public opposition. Ethical: the generation that benefits from the power should deal with its waste, but also not foreclose future options (retrievability).

items.stem: Distinguish between the moderator and the control rods.
items.answer: The moderator slows neutrons (without absorbing them) to make fission more likely; control rods absorb neutrons to reduce the number available for fission.

items.stem: Explain why the decay heat of a reactor must be removed even after the chain reaction has stopped.
items.answer: Fission products continue to decay, initially producing about 6–7 % of full thermal power; without cooling the fuel overheats and can melt.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an uncontrolled chain reaction and a controlled chain reaction.
items.answer: In a controlled reaction (reactor) the multiplication factor is held at exactly 1 by control rods; in an uncontrolled one (weapon) k > 1 and the number of fissions grows exponentially in microseconds.

items.stem: Isabel writes four statements while revising nuclear reactor components: moderator, control rods and heat exchanger. Which one is a misconception?

items.stem: Distinguish between low-level waste and high-level waste.
items.answer: Low-level waste has low activity and little heat output and can be compacted and buried near the surface; high-level waste is intensely radioactive and hot, requiring cooling, vitrification and deep geological disposal.

items.stem: Compare graphite-moderated and light-water-moderated reactors in terms of the fuel enrichment required, the number of collisions needed to thermalise neutrons and safety considerations.
items.answer: Graphite (carbon, 12 u) keeps ~84 % of neutron energy per collision, needing ~110 collisions, but absorbs very few neutrons, so natural or slightly enriched uranium can be used; it is flammable at high temperature. Light water (hydrogen, 1 u) thermalises in ~20 collisions but absorbs more neutrons, needing ~3–5 % enriched fuel; if the water boils away the moderation is lost and the reaction slows (negative void coefficient), an inherent safety feature, whereas in some graphite designs (RBMK) loss of water increased reactivity.
items.markingKey: Collision fractions and numbers (A1 A1); absorption and enrichment (R1); void coefficient / safety (R1); balanced conclusion (R1).

items.stem: A sample of vitrified waste contains caesium-137 (half-life 30.2 y) with activity 1000 GBq and plutonium-239 (half-life 24 100 y) with activity 60 GBq. (c) Explain why the long-term hazard of waste is dominated by actinides even though fission products are initially far more active. (d) Discuss one implication for repository design.
items.answer: (a) Cs-137 101 GBq, Pu-239 59.8 GBq; (b) Cs-137; (c) short-lived fission products decay away within centuries; long half-life actinides remain; (d) barriers must last ~10⁵ years
items.markingKey: (a) A = A₀(1/2)^(t/T½) for each (M1): 101 GBq and 59.8 GBq (A1 A1). (b) comparison (A1). (c) half-life argument (R1). (d) repository implication, e.g. long-lived containment, stable geology (R1).

items.stem: A nuclear power station produces 1000 MW of electrical power with an overall efficiency of 35 %. Each fission of U-235 releases 200 MeV. (a) Calculate the thermal power of the reactor. (d) Compare with the mass of coal (energy density 30 MJ kg⁻¹) needed for the same thermal output, and comment.
items.answer: (a) 2.86 × 10⁹ W; (b) 8.93 × 10¹⁹ s⁻¹; (c) 1100 kg; (d) 3.01 × 10⁹ kg of coal – about 2.7 × 10⁶ times more

items.stem: A reactor designer considers beryllium (9 u) as a moderator. In an average collision a neutron keeps a fraction f = 0.820 of its kinetic energy (averaged over collision angles). (b) Estimate the number of collisions needed to slow a 2.0 MeV neutron to 0.025 eV. (c) Other than the number of collisions, state and explain two properties the designer must consider.
items.answer: (b) about 92 collisions; (c) neutron absorption cross-section, cost/availability, ability to act as coolant, chemical/fire safety

items.stem: Explain the difference between neutron-induced fission and spontaneous fission.
items.answer: Spontaneous fission happens randomly without an external trigger (rare except in very heavy nuclides); induced fission follows absorption of a neutron, forming an excited compound nucleus (e.g. U-236) that splits.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Water is the best choice of moderator for a nuclear reactor."
items.answer: Light water is practical and widely used, but the best moderator depends on fuel enrichment and safety design.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: hydrogen nuclei slow neutrons in few collisions; water is cheap and also acts as coolant. Arguments against: ordinary hydrogen absorbs some neutrons, requiring enriched fuel; heavy water or graphite allow natural uranium; graphite can burn (Windscale, Chernobyl). Supported judgement: Light water is practical and widely used, but the best moderator depends on fuel enrichment and safety design.

items.stem: "Nuclear power should be part of the solution to climate change despite the problems of waste and safety." Discuss.
items.answer: Many energy analysts see a role for nuclear power alongside renewables; the judgement depends on weighing low-carbon reliability against waste, cost and risk.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: very low lifecycle CO₂ emissions; reliable baseload power; small land use and fuel volume. Arguments against: long-lived waste with no operating repository in most countries; rare but severe accidents; high construction cost and long build times; proliferation concerns. Supported judgement: Many energy analysts see a role for nuclear power alongside renewables; the judgement depends on weighing low-carbon reliability against waste, cost and risk.
